name: Battle of Lundy's Lane
place: Lundy's Lane, by the Falls of Niagara, Upper Canada (Ontario)

features.name: to DeCew's Falls and Twelve Mile Creek

units.name: 9th and 22nd US Infantry (Scott's brigade)
units.commander: Col. Hugh Brady; Maj. Henry Leavenworth

units.name: Towson's company, US Artillery: two 6-pounders and a 5.5-inch howitzer
23rd US Infantry (Ripley's brigade)
units.commander: Maj. Daniel McFarland; Brig. Gen. Eleazer Ripley

units.name: Ritchie's and Biddle's companies, US Artillery
units.commander: Maj. Jacob Hindman; Capts. John Ritchie and Thomas Biddle

units.name: Porter's brigade: New York and Pennsylvania volunteers and Canadian Volunteers
1st Militia Brigade: 1st, 2nd, 4th and 5th Lincoln and 2nd York
Royal Artillery: two 6-pounders and a 5.5-inch howitzer, with Congreve rockets

events.title: The Niagara, July 1814
events.text: Brown's army crossed the Niagara on 3 July and took Fort Erie. On the 5th it beat Riall at Chippawa, about 6 km south of here, then moved up to Fort George, and by the 24th it was back in camp on the plain between Street's Creek and the Chippawa. At midnight Pearson got orders to advance with the light brigade. Merritt reached Lundy's Lane with part of his troop at three in the morning and went on as far as Bridgewater; a few dragoons rode on to the Falls to look at the camp at Chippawa.

events.title: The high ground
events.text: By seven Pearson's light brigade, about 800 of all ranks, has taken the high ground at Lundy's Lane. The lane leaves the Queenston road almost at a right angle and runs west past a meeting-house on the highest point of the rise, with the graveyard beside it. A young orchard covers the slope below the graveyard to the Portage road. Two six-pounders stand near the church.

events.title: A picket at Mrs. Wilson's
events.text: At eight, Merritt writes, they fall back on Lundy's Lane, leaving an advanced picket at Mrs. Wilson's, a small tavern near Table Rock. Drummond, who sailed from York in the schooner Netley on the evening of the 24th, reached the mouth of the river at daybreak and sent Tucker along the other bank toward Lewiston.

events.title: Lewiston
events.text: About noon Tucker's column takes Lewiston, on the American bank, and drives out the garrison. Swift sends Brown an express: the enemy holds Lewiston and is thought to be advancing on Schlosser. In the course of the morning Riall rode forward to join Pearson, and directed the advance of Colonel Hercules Scott's brigade and part of the reserve.

events.title: For Queenston
events.text: At four Brown orders Scott to march on Queenston, and to report at once if he meets the enemy in force. The brigade, about 1,080 men, is on the road over the King's Bridge in less than thirty minutes after dinner, with Towson's guns and Harris's dragoons, meaning to make no halt short of Queenston.

events.title: Mrs. Wilson's
events.text: At five the British see the Americans coming, and the advance picket is driven in. At Mrs. Wilson's the British officers come out, mount their horses and ride off as Scott comes up. Riall orders the militia and the light brigade to retreat; the main army, Merritt writes, is several miles in the rear.

events.title: Drummond
events.text: Towards six a dragoon meets Drummond on the road from Queenston with Riall's message. Drummond turns Morrison's column back from the Beaver Dam road and orders the guns up. He finds the light brigade retiring, countermands it and forms his line: the guns on the summit of the hill, his two brass 24-pounders a little in front of the centre; the 89th, the Royal Scots detachment and the 41st light company in the rear of the hill; the Glengarry on the right; the Incorporated Militia and the King's on the left of the great road, the dragoons in rear of the left.

events.title: Out of the wood
events.text: Scott passes the wood. The 9th, 11th and 22nd deploy in the fields on the left of the road and the 25th on the right, and Towson's guns unlimber on the highway. The sun is about half an hour high, Cruikshank writes, between six and seven, when Scott begins the engagement; the witnesses put the first shots anywhere from six to a quarter past seven.

events.title: The attack on the hill
events.text: Scott sends the 11th and 22nd straight at the hill and the 9th and 25th round its flanks. The Glengarry and the Incorporated Militia, 700 strong by Merritt's count, take the first fire. A shell from the British battery strikes one of Towson's ammunition wagons, which blows up. The sun sets at half past seven.

events.title: Riall taken
events.text: Jesup's 25th makes a wide circuit through the undergrowth, hidden by the thickets, and enters the gap of more than two hundred yards between the British left and the bank. It strikes the Incorporated Militia in the flank and holds the Queenston road behind the British left. Drummond's aide Loring is taken, then Riall, badly wounded in the shoulder, as he comes back along the road. Lisle's dragoons fall back a mile and a half, to Muddy Run. It is getting dark: at twenty yards, Merritt writes, friends cannot be told from enemies.

events.title: To pieces
events.text: The musketry goes on until half past eight. The 11th and 22nd go entirely to pieces, and the 9th alone keeps its formation. Scott's brigade has borne the brunt for an hour and a half; by nine it is down from about 1,000 men to 600. The British guns fire on from the summit.

events.title: Nine o'clock
events.text: About nine there is a lull. Ripley's and Porter's brigades come up the road to reinforce Scott, and Brown comes up last with the reserve. At the same hour the head of Colonel Hercules Scott's column, fourteen miles from Twelve Mile Creek under a burning sun, comes in view on the extreme right along the lane, and forms a second line in rear of Lundy's Lane. Porter put the men he carried into the field at less than 300.

events.title: I'll try, Sir
events.text: Ripley's brigade forms in the hollow, hidden by the dark. 'I'll try, Sir,' says Miller. His 21st, short of three hundred men by his own count, advances silently in line up a ravine screened by the church and thickets to a stout log fence within twenty yards of the guns, fires one volley and rushes the battery. It carries the height and the cannon. The 1st gives way under point-blank fire and retires in disorder, then re-forms; the 23rd advances with admirable firmness and loses heavily, McFarland killed. Porter is on their left, the 25th in the thickets on the right.

events.title: By moonlight
events.text: 'It was then evening, but moonlight,' Miller writes; the moon is up, but its light is faint and uncertain through drifting smoke and dust. Drummond's first counterattack is repelled with heavy loss. The 103rd marches in the darkness straight into the centre of the American position, and the lines are scarcely ever more than twenty yards apart.

events.title: Scott's last charge
events.text: The artillery goes on until half past ten, Allen writes, and then comes a charge. Scott leads a column of about 250 men past the guns. The 89th is repulsed at about twenty paces; Ripley's men fire into the column's rear, and it breaks. Scott is wounded by a musket ball that fractures his shoulder, and about the same time Brown takes a flesh wound in the thigh.

events.title: Almost midnight
events.text: When it is almost midnight the last attack, headed by the light company of the 41st under Captain Glew, reaches the summit and recovers the guns. The Americans could not take them off: Dr Bull saw 60 to 70 horses lying near Miller's captured battery.

events.title: Back to camp
events.text: The Americans hold the ground until twelve, Allen writes, then fall back to their camp, more than two miles. Brown, exhausted by loss of blood, hands over to Ripley, who withdraws under cover of desultory firing. The British take an American field-piece and throw themselves down to rest among the dead and dying. The moon sets soon after midnight.

events.title: Ripley comes back
events.text: Brown ordered Ripley to meet and beat the enemy if he appeared at dawn; the order was not executed. In the morning Ripley comes back over the Chippawa with about 1,200 men to bury the dead and recover the wounded, and finds the field occupied in force by his antagonist.

events.title: The bridge and the mills
events.text: Ripley retires, destroying the bridge behind him. The Americans set fire to Street's Mills and burn the mills at Bridgewater, and by noon they have left the field; that night the army reaches Fort Erie and entrenches. The British return counts 84 killed, 559 wounded and 193 missing; the American return 171 killed, 572 wounded and 117 missing. It is the bloodiest battle of the war.

outcome.result: Drawn: the Americans carried the hill and its guns, then withdrew to the Chippawa at midnight, and Drummond held the field
losses: 860 by the official return of 30 July: 171 killed, 572 wounded and 117 missing, among the wounded Brown, Scott and Porter. Revised counts give 174 killed, 572 wounded, 79 captured and 28 missing. Scott's four regiments lost 505 of them, Ripley's three 226. The missing are not drawn.

878 by the British return: 84 killed, 559 wounded, 193 missing and 42 prisoners, among them Riall taken and Drummond wounded. The 89th lost 254, the Royal Scots 172 and the Incorporated Militia 125. Revised counts give 84 killed, 559 wounded, 169 captured and 55 missing. The missing are not drawn.
outcome.note: Both sides claimed the field. The clock times are officers' watches, and they disagree by up to an hour on when the fighting began. Every strength below the brigade is split from Graves's brigade totals, and when each unit lost its men is placed by the phases it fought in.

sources: E. A. Cruikshank, ed., The Documentary History of the Campaign upon the Niagara Frontier in 1814, Part I (Lundy's Lane Historical Society, 1896): Drummond's report of 27 July, the District General Order of 26 July, the British return of killed, wounded and missing by corps, Brown's report of 7 August with the list of prisoners, and the letters of Allen, Miller, Porter, Sawyer, Bull, Varnum, Hercules Scott and an officer at Fort Erie.

E. A. Cruikshank, The Battle of Lundy's Lane, 25th July, 1814: a historical study, 3rd ed. (Lundy's Lane Historical Society, 1893): the ground, the dispositions, the hours, and both official returns by corps.

William Hamilton Merritt's journal, in William Wood, ed., Select British Documents of the Canadian War of 1812, vol. III (Champlain Society, 1926-28): the morning at Bridgewater, the picket at Mrs. Wilson's, the dark and Riall's capture.
Winfield Scott, Memoirs of Lieut.-General Scott, vol. I (1864), ch. XI: the march after dinner and the last charge. Written fifty years after.

'Explanation of Sketch of Action of the 25th July, 1814', enclosed in Prevost's despatch to Bathurst of 5 August 1814, in An Account of the Battle of Lundy's Lane (1853; reprinted 1947): the lettered key to the British positions; the sketch itself was not seen.

Places from OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL): Drummond Hill Cemetery and church, Lundy's Lane, Main Street and Portage Road, the Falls, the Bridgewater mills plaque, Chippawa. Sunrise, sunset and the moon computed for the place and date, local mean time.

What is reconstructed: the 1814 junction of the lane and the road from today's streets, a few hundred yards east of the church; Mrs. Wilson's tavern, the hollow, the log fence, Skinner's lane, Jesup's track, the wood Scott passed and the thickets toward the bank from the sources' descriptions, within about 200 m. Regimental strengths below the brigade, the hours of Riall's capture and Miller's charge, and Scott's halt short of the wood are placed from the order of events; Graves's maps and returns would settle them.
